posts.author: AnneLost
posts.body: Hello guys, I'm on the very beginning of my project and still mapping so I thought to ask first, how do you guys layout a map? How do you make it functional but also convey a story and atmosphere without being so direct the player knows ah this part is a game mechanic or something before its even the time to use it. Thank you for the answers

posts.author: DevRPG2k
posts.body:
I played a lot of JRPGs from the 2D era and games made with RPG Maker. I often used screenshots to try to replicate them and thus be able to practice. Over time, this becomes easier. Today, I'm still not good, but I don't have that feeling that I won't be able to do anything because I don't know where to start.
Sometimes I look at a map of a real city or a game and think about how it could work and try to apply it to the plot of a game.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
You start with a list.
Write the "theme" of the map on top, and then list everything you need on the map in that list.
Depending on the game this might be from several points of view (Logistically a house needs a bathroom or outhouse, story-wise it needs beds for everyone living there including the names of the NPCs, and from a game mechanic you'll need certain shops in a village and so on.
Give that list at least three iterations if needed - which means you go over the list on three different days and work on something else between those times to make sure you're not missing something.
Then take pen and paper and make a sketch of what to place where on the map - expect to get the size wrong and having to redesign the map if you're inexperienced in mapping.
only after you have that sketch open the editor and start making the map and filling it with content

posts.author: Crim_T
posts.body:
If you haven't seen them before, the Yanfly comics have some interesting points on map creation.  Chapter 3 (Let's Make a Dungeon) & Chapter 4  (Let's Make a Town) are a fun read and fairly relevant.
http://yanfly.moe/comics/
As you're probably aware, Avery has some absolutely fantastic mapping tutorials.  Just off the top of my head, the tutorial on mapping forests and the tutorial on mapping rivers were extremely helpful for me personally.
Tutorials | The Official RPG Maker Blog
Tutorials articles from the the Official RPG Maker Blog
www.rpgmakerweb.com
RMMZ Tutorials
forums.rpgmakerweb.com
As far as my own advice is worth... The best thing to remember is that it's extremely easy to adjust the map (At least in MZ) with RPG Maker.  Getting a prototype started is important, so don't worry about it being "pefect" the first try.
Lately, for the larger more involved maps, I've also been liking starting a minimap just with outlines.  Often using the overworld tilest to get an idea of how the flow of the map will work, and if it makes sense within the setting, before starting on the real version.

posts.author: Danatoth
posts.body:
I basically just make everything function as it would in real life. Why would this dungeon exist? Is it a tunnel system that goes through this mountain? Why does it curve this way? Is there harder stone they have to go around? Why was it easier than going over the mountain? Could the cave collapse and cause the player to go over the mountain later to get back, thus showing harder enemies? That could explain why they went through the mountain.
Where is this town getting its food? You did add farms nearby right? Why does this town have X shops? Where do the people live? Etc. I just ask myself these questions and maps generally explain themselves to me in their layout.

Ooh, I like this advice! It's a very similar mentality to how I'm making mine; I sort of let the map join itself together after creating a rough outline of A, to B, to C, to D storyline, then use spontaneous storytelling to make the world feel 'believable'!
Also having a consistent style so the player gets used to navigation and maybe even what to expect when progressing through your game can give confidence to the game's craftsmanship.

posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body:
When I started with RPG Maker I did some tutorials which at least got me started. (I think the tutorials were for RPG Maker VX.) They gave advice which I tended to follow afterwards, although I changed many of the things that I did things later.
I concur with deciding what the map will do for the game first (for example, provide a location for a shopkeeper, a "starter dungeon" for the player learn the combat mechanisms and increase the party experience, a safe town with basic services such as shops and an inn, a town with services but which needs exploring and enemies fought).
Practice will help you understand how to use the tiles. People can tell you about "shift-pasting" auto-tiles, but, if you are like me, you have to to it a few times for it to stick in your brain.
My personal advice is that small maps are a lot easier to do than large maps, so, 1) don't make your maps larger than they need to be, and 2) consider splitting maps into several smaller ones linked by doors or transfers.

posts.author: ASimpleShrine550
posts.body:
The real way, is to properly coordinate the map location then in visual editing to layer the art and path.
There is more than one way to peel an orange, with all Roads leading to Rome. You can plan the map on paper with things like (Home lower left, Mountains High Right, Castle in middle, Dungeon scattered throughout.)
All maps you use in your project can be simplified (implied) objectives instead of photo realism if you like the feel of map making. If you are artistic enough, you can layer tiles with your own arts (sprites, drawings, e.t.c.) into the map project to add your own style.
Depends on genre of map making we choose. [Most will stick with Top View type styles as default. But customizers can choose Isometric, 2.5D with 3D add ons, Mimicry/Simulations/Parodies of actual locations.] You may want to choose your map to be made with the style you choose your project to be. [you know a RPG Maker Horror Action Shooter you will need to think survival maps, maze and tricks, jump scares, cut scenes, meaningful dialogue, action heavy locations and classic dungeon crawler where the maps can give thrills, excitement, to give your players to "Take On The Target Clear The Objective and Finish to the Flag", or if you want to make your own clone of your favorite monster creatures series. You would have to design your maps to reflect the towns settings, the character interactions, the monster fights, the rewards, where the map makes sense to the RPG elements no matter how explorative or massive. Or if you even want to design some dating sim, you would still need to have maps with background scenes that have good art to progress story setting (Romance at college class, The Club mishap, The Date at the Lake, Make Out Valley, A Cheaters Way Out on the Highway.) You know every map you put into your project should serve purpose rather than filler space. It's natural to have test and debug rooms filled with every little thing to make everything work proper before throwing all your eggs into one basket.]
Conveying depth will make your settings more believable. Just randomly make rooms to get a feel, then maybe Photoshop on your favorite editor additionals to give it a lively touch.
Or do the little brother thing where you just randomly click things in doodle mode even if it looks like crud you can still make something actually quite decent (or boringly hilarious) for just messing around.
The point is to have a feel rather than perfect. Unless you're truly artistic with skills that can't quite get that perfect green pixel to the finishing touch well my good friend I feel your pain. Don't pet perfectionism on the head, push it aside for some free range creativity once in a while.
I don't know how many of you have been in the actual bizz but I assume most of you are in the true know. About putting together the true work even behind simple projects and having to do things from the ground up professionally.
But, if you can make a map at all just by photo-editing tile art. You impressed me already, keep up the good work to you all. Happy Spriting!
